hits.name: Bryan Johnson
hits.text:
I reviewed Tobi’s biomarker’s from the car race yesterday. His heart rate, respiration, nervous system, focus, brain state, and more.

It’s insane.

I have some observations below. First, you need to get into the right headspace to understand the insanity.

Imagine this…

> you're breathing at an 8 min/mile (5 min/km) pace
> in a 110°F (43°C) heat chamber 
> heart rate of 145 bpm, peaking at 171 bpm
> intermittently body checked 700 lbs (320 kg) of force
> your core body temp near 102°F (39°C), a high fever
> claustrophobically strapped in a six point harness 
> helmeted head weighs 65 lbs (30 kg) under g load
> no evaporative cooling
> you’ve lost 4.6% of your body mass through sweat
> you can’t move
> vision narrowing from thermal strain and dehydration

Now, in these circumstances, your job is to…

> drive a tightrope at 180 mph (290 km/h)
> overtaking/defending against ahead, beside, behind
> staying within millimeters of tolerance 
> lose concentration for a tenth of a sec, in trouble

Do this for 2.5 hours straight.

A few additional things I find interesting from looking at the data:

1. It’s crazy to me his body can be in such a heightened state while completely stationary. Sitting down, he produced a cardiac load equal to high intensity physical exertion.

2. Thirty minutes before the race, Tobi’s body was already racing. His heart rate elevated to 136 bpm, more than 2x his baseline.

3. In qualifying, the higher his heart rate, the faster his lap. Arousal and performance moved in sync, including his personal best lap.

4. He lost 4.6% of his body mass in sweat. This is severe dehydration. At 2% dehydration your reaction time measurably decreases. He surpassed this in the first hour.

5. His nervous system was switched entirely to fight. There was no chill, anywhere.

6. His incredibly high breathing rate was driven by extreme sympathetic stress and rising core temperature, averaging 41 breaths a minute on his flying laps, moving 93 liters of air a minute.

7. His peak respiratory rate was 59. This is an all out sprint!

8. The only life experience I can map onto Tobi’s experience  was doing 27 mg of 5-MeO-DMT, the world’s most powerful psychedelic. It was all consuming, taking me to the cliff of my physical and mental capacity for 45 minutes. Otherwise, it is very hard for me to imagine being able to excel in these extreme conditions for 2.5 hours.
|
I now understand a little more what Tobi was telling me about the flow state he drops into. Under such extreme physiological conditions, the brain ruthlessly narrows focus. His brain downregulates the self-monitoring prefrontal regions (the self narration). The spike in norepinephrine dilates time, creating the perception of time slowing down.

MRIs on professional drivers show they use roughly one brain region for tasks where novices light up fifteen. A novice would be crushed in these circumstances in less than 10 minutes.

I’m impressed. It’s very hard and nearly impossible to actually understand what it’s like to go through something like this. 

Tobi and @dhh (Tobi’s teammate) were both my first customers at Braintree and gave my startup life when it wasn’t clear if we had a future. They generously encouraged other startups in the Ruby on Rails community to use us.  DHH’s co-founder @jasonfried  did as well. They’ve been great friends to me.

As to Tobi’s performance in the race, he did exceptionally well:

> closed within +0.51% of the fastest Bronze driver, putting him neck and neck with the top ranked amateur drivers in North America

> got his fastest lap of the race on Lap 88 (1:15.359), over two hours in and with peak dehydration and thermal strain, showing incredible tenacity

> finished just +2.60% off absolute class best, competing against world class professionals

There were 150 drivers competing in this race. Respect to all of you. I have a whole new appreciation for the sport.

hits.name: Dr. Rhonda Patrick
hits.text:
I use exogenous ketones. But not everyday.

I use them strategically, especially before situations when stress could interfere with how clearly I think.

Human studies suggest that exogenous ketones such as beta-hydroxybutyrate may have anxiolytic effects and support cognitive function during stress. One proposed reason is that ketones influence inhibitory signaling involving GABA and adenosine, which may help quiet some of the "mental noise" produced by anxiety.

Before a major presentation or podcast, I'll take about 10 mL of a liquid beta-hydroxybutyrate ester (about 3-5 grams of ketones). For me, it helps calm some of that anxiety and improves my focus and attention.

I view exogenous ketones as a situational tool, not a daily supplement, and I've found them extremely helpful when I need to perform under pressure.

hits.name: Eric Topol
Dr. Rhonda Patrick
hits.text:
About 1 in 8 children and adolescents were diagnosed with vitamin D deficiency within a year of starting a GLP-1 drug.

Nearly 17% received at least one new diagnosis of a nutritional deficiency or related complication. Vitamin D deficiency alone affected 12.4%. Yet fewer than one in four received nutrition counseling within six months.

This doesn't prove the medications caused the deficiencies (obesity itself increases the risk of low vitamin D). But GLP-1 drugs suppress appetite by design, and when the body is undergoing rapid growth and development, nutritional sufficiency matters enormously.

Vitamin D supports calcium absorption and skeletal development, along with muscle function, immune regulation, and neurodevelopment.

The takeaway here is not that children should avoid GLP-1 drugs when appropriate. It’s that treatment should include nutrition counseling and monitoring of vitamin D and iron status, protein intake, and growth, not just weight loss.

PS: Adults using GLP-1 drugs should pay attention to micronutrient status, too!
hits.draft_en:
Rhonda Patrick flagged a study: about 1 in 8 kids on weight-loss jabs ended up low in vitamin D within a year, and few got any nutrition advice.

Her note at the end is for the rest of us. Adults on these drugs should watch it too.

If the jab means you're barely eating, what you do eat matters more. Get your protein in, ask your doctor about a blood test, and don't judge it on the scales alone.

hits.name: Nick Norwitz MD PhD
hits.text:
A Better Fasting-Mimicking Diet

Some astute readers have pointed out that the way I would formulate a fasting-mimicking diet is different from the formulation used in the original research, which is calorically restricted, low in protein, and contains roughly equal parts fat and carbohydrate (9% protein, 44% fat, and 47% carbohydrate).

However, please note the explicit purpose of a fasting-mimicking diet: to mimic the physiology and metabolic signature of fasting, including lower levels of IGF-1, insulin, and glucose, and higher levels of ketones.

Therefore, it seems only sensible to swap some of the carbohydrate fraction for more healthy fats. There’s every reason to expect this would produce a stronger fasting-like metabolic effect than a mixed-macronutrient, low-calorie diet.

If you force me to guess why the original fasting-mimicking diet protocol was based on this particular macronutrient split, I’d suspect it was because it’s easier to get people to comply with, easier to formulate and commercialize, or some combination thereof.

But from a metabolic standpoint, if your goal is to mimic fasting physiology, olive oil, walnuts, olives, and egg yolks are going to get you closer to that metabolic state than relatively higher-carbohydrate foods.

hits.name: Benjamin Bikman
hits.text:
Did you know that a fast actually increases your metabolic rate? It's a myth that your metabolism slows the moment you stop eating. Early in a fast, it actually does the opposite. 

As blood glucose tends to drift down when you stop eating, your body releases more norepinephrine (a close cousin of epinephrine/adrenaline), and your resting energy expenditure climbs up. In healthy adults who fasted for 84 hours, resting energy expenditure rose about 14% by day three, while norepinephrine more than doubled. 

Of course, the more adrenaline and its sibling rise, the more they inhibit insulin release. This further amplifies the metabolic rate effect, insofar as insulin slows metabolic rate very well. 

This is clearly not "starvation mode." There is simply a metabolic cost to your body mobilizing fuel and keeping you alive while you take a break from food.
hits.draft_en:
Ben Bikman says skipping a meal doesn't put your body into "starvation mode." In one study, resting energy use went up about 14% by day three of a fast.

Nobody's saying do a three-day fast on a building site. That's a good way to fall off something.

But a late breakfast or a lighter lunch won't wreck your metabolism. If you're not hungry, you don't have to eat just because it's smoko. Stay hydrated and stay safe on the job.

hits.name: Nick Norwitz MD PhD
hits.text:
Did you know you can gain strength while fasting? 

Like this guy, who added 10 pounds to his bench press while on a fat-only fast.

Here’s the deal: you’re not necessarily building muscle. But muscular strength isn’t determined just by how much muscle you have. It also depends on how effectively your nervous system plugs into your muscles and recruits muscle fibers.

In other words, strength has a major neural component.

So, if an intervention changes your nervous system state, it’s entirely feasible to see improvements in functional strength without eating a single gram of protein.

The caveat, of course, is that indefinite protein restriction has a negative side effect, which we call death.

I would suggest avoiding that.
hits.media_note: image (2) + quote post of @nicknorwitz (fasting mimicking diet thread)
hits.draft_en:
Nick Norwitz made a point worth knowing: strength isn't only about how much muscle you've got. It's also how well your nerves switch the muscle on.

That's good news past 50. Practice makes you stronger before the muscle even grows.

So practise the lift. Same movement, good form, a few times a week. Your body learns it. Just don't skip the protein while you're at it.

outsiders.text:
Jack Ma told Elon Musk humans will always be smarter than machines. 

Musk’s reaction says everything.

“Computers may be very clever, but human beings are much smarter. We invented the computer. I've never seen a computer invent a human being.”

Ma's argument was simple. Computers are tools. They calculate faster, remember more, but humans still hold something machines don't: experience, judgment, wisdom.

Musk clearly didn't buy it. “What would be an example of something that humans are better than a computer at?”

Watching this exchange now feels completely different than it did then. AI agents aren't just calculating anymore. They're writing code, analyzing documents, planning tasks, deciding what to do next on their own.

METR found that the length of software tasks frontier agents can complete autonomously has historically doubled roughly every seven months, with signs of even faster progress through parts of 2024.

That's where Ma's argument starts to buckle. For decades, technology automated what humans did. AI is starting to automate what we assumed required a human to think.

And companies were already learning to create enormous value with almost no people before this wave even arrived. Instagram sold for $1 billion with 13 employees. WhatsApp sold for $19 billion with 55.

Now picture what happens when a small team can direct hundreds of machines that never sleep, never take a salary, never need an office.

The question was never just which jobs disappear.

It's what happens to the money once fewer humans are needed to create it in the first place.

That's the question behind 2028: The Economy Without Humans.

Who gets the money when machines do the work?

this is pure f*cking treasure

A Stanford research group found how to orchestrate Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra together, and it completely breaks the resampling wall

most developers think test-time compute means running 32 blind retries on one model. you burn API tokens repeating the same 2-3 error clusters in loops

Stanford's paper (arXiv:2608.05643) splits the compute between two different brains:

> breadth search: GPT-6 Astra runs high-entropy exploration (T=0.8) to discover divergent solution paths
> step audit: Claude Opus 5.5 scans each step at T=0.0 and catches the exact logic fallacy
> local surgery: Opus rewrites only the broken step instead of dumping the whole reasoning chain
> verifier-free consensus: majority voting locks the proof without relying on drift-prone PRMs

the benchmark metrics outclass standard Best-of-N sampling:

> 91.2% recovery rate on detected reasoning flaws
> under 1.8% regressions on correct branches
> MATH500 jumps from 29.6% to 58.0% (+28.4% absolute gain)
> AMC-2023 improves by +7.5% with zero reward models

Astra explores the maze. Opus repairs the logic

you stop burning tokens on blind retries. you run verified reasoning depth
